opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I thought that was one of the more interesting results to come out in a while, partly because it cut against what a lot of people, including me, would have predicted. The headline was that experienced open-source developers, working on large codebases they knew really well, were slower with AI tools than without them. And yet they *believed* they'd been sped up. That gap between perception and reality is, to me, almost the more important finding.

I'd interpret it with a few caveats. First, this was a specific setting: very experienced people, on mature repositories they'd worked on for years, with lots of implicit context and high quality standards. That's close to the worst case for these tools. The AI doesn't have the tacit knowledge in the developer's head, so you spend time prompting, reviewing, correcting, and cleaning up output that doesn't quite fit. For a newcomer to a codebase, or for greenfield prototyping, I'd expect the picture to look quite different.

Second, it was a snapshot of tools at a particular moment. Capabilities have been moving fast, especially on longer-horizon agentic tasks, so I wouldn't treat one study as a permanent fact about AI and productivity. It's a data point on a moving curve.

But third, and this is where I think it should update people, it's a real warning against relying on vibes. A lot of the case for "AI is already massively accelerating everything" rests on self-reports, and this study suggests self-reports can be badly off, even in sign. That matters for forecasting. If you're trying to figure out when AI starts meaningfully speeding up AI research itself, which is the crux of a lot of my scenarios, you want careful measurement, not anecdotes from people who feel faster.

So for me it nudged things a bit toward "the takeoff starts somewhat later or more gradually than the most aggressive views implied." I don't think it overturns the broader trend, because benchmark performance on long tasks has kept climbing. But it highlights a gap between doing well on clean, well-specified tasks and actually being useful in the messy real world, and how fast that gap closes is one of the key uncertainties right now.

r001.rationale: It says the result applies to experienced developers on mature codebases and expects a different picture for newcomers, greenfield prototyping, and other settings.

r002.rationale: It says self-reports can be badly off, even in sign, but does not clearly state a general bias toward overestimating AI productivity gains.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss a 25% speedup on one-hour tasks or compare that with one-month tasks.

r004.rationale: It says the finding nudges its view toward a takeoff that starts later or more gradually, linking limited current productivity evidence to slower substantial acceleration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was a really interesting result, and I think it's worth being careful about what it does and doesn't show. The setup, as I understand it, was: take experienced open-source developers working in their own large, mature codebases that they know intimately, randomize tasks to "AI allowed" versus "AI not allowed," and measure how long the tasks took. And the finding was that with AI, they were something like 19 percent slower, while believing they'd been sped up. That gap between perceived and actual speedup is maybe the most striking part.

My first reaction is that this is a legitimate update against the more breathless claims you hear, where people say "I'm ten times more productive now." For that population, on that kind of task, in early-to-mid 2025, that just wasn't true. And I think we should take that seriously rather than explain it away.

But I'd also say it's a pretty narrow slice. These were people with years of deep context on their specific repos, which is roughly the worst case for a model that has to come in cold. The gains people report tend to be largest when you're working in unfamiliar territory, or doing greenfield work, or writing boilerplate, or in domains where you personally are weak. And the models in the study are already getting superseded. So I'd interpret it as "current tools, for experts on their home turf, roughly break even or slightly hurt," not "AI doesn't help programmers."

The part I find most relevant to my own worldview is the self-report problem. People felt faster when they weren't. That should make us more skeptical of anecdotal productivity claims in both directions, including the claims coming out of frontier labs about how much their own research is being accelerated. I lean on those a bit in thinking about timelines, and this is a reason to discount them somewhat and to want more studies like METR's, ideally repeated every few months so we can actually see the trend rather than arguing about one snapshot.

And honestly, it did move me. Not enormously, but it's one of the things that nudged my median timelines somewhat later over the past year. If the loop of AI speeding up AI research were really kicking in hard already, I'd expect it to show up more clearly in careful measurements like this one. It hasn't yet. That's evidence the takeoff is a bit further off than I'd thought, though the trend in task horizon lengths that METR also tracks still looks pretty steep to me, so I wouldn't overcorrect either.

r001.rationale: The response calls the study a narrow slice and says its result for experts on familiar codebases does not mean AI cannot help programmers in other settings.

r002.rationale: It says developers felt faster when they were actually slower, and argues that this should make us more skeptical of productivity claims.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss a 25% speedup, one-hour tasks, or how speedups might change for one-month tasks.

r004.rationale: It says the lack of clear measured acceleration is evidence that AI takeoff is further off than the speaker had thought.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s evidence that we should take seriously, especially because it pushes against the temptation to assume that better performance on coding benchmarks automatically translates into greater productivity.

But I’d distinguish two questions. One is whether these tools help experienced programmers do their actual work today. The other is how quickly AI capabilities are improving, and what that implies about future systems. A finding that programmers were slowed down is directly relevant to the first question, but it doesn’t settle the second.

An experienced programmer has a lot of context about their codebase. If the AI produces something that takes longer to review and fix than it would have taken to write, using it can make you slower even if the output looks impressive. That’s a real limitation, not something we should wave away.

So I’d update against claims that current coding assistants are already delivering large productivity gains across the board. And I’d want to see whether that result persists as the tools improve. The important thing is to measure actual outcomes, rather than infer usefulness from either benchmark scores or people’s enthusiasm.

r001.rationale: The response says the finding does not settle questions about future systems, but does not say that it leaves room for speedups in other coding settings.

r002.rationale: It cautions against assuming benchmark performance means productivity gains and against claims of large gains across the board, but does not state a general bias toward overestimating those gains.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss a 25% speedup on one-hour tasks or extrapolate to one-month tasks.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes current productivity from future capability, but does not argue that negligible speedups today would imply more time before AI substantially accelerates development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an important result, and it should update us against the idea that today’s AI tools are already making everyone dramatically more productive. But I’d be careful about generalising from it. These were experienced programmers working in codebases they knew well. That’s a setting where they have a lot of context that the AI doesn’t, and where checking and correcting the AI’s work can eat up the time it saves.

One particularly interesting aspect is that the programmers thought the tools were helping, even though they were actually taking longer. So people’s impressions of how useful these systems are aren’t necessarily reliable. We need measurements like this.

For the question I’m most concerned about—when AI could substantially accelerate AI research—that’s relevant evidence, but it doesn’t settle things. You’d want to know which tasks the systems can do, how much supervision they need, and how those things change with the next generation. A finding that current tools slow down one group of programmers is compatible with future systems being much more useful. But you shouldn’t just assume that improvement; you should test it.

r001.rationale: It says the finding should not be generalized from experienced programmers in familiar codebases and is compatible with future systems being more useful.

r002.rationale: It says participants thought the tools helped despite taking longer, and that impressions are not necessarily reliable. It does not state a general bias toward overestimating productivity gains.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss a 25% speedup, one-hour tasks, or infer greater speedups from handling one-month tasks.

r004.rationale: It says current tools slowing one group does not settle future usefulness, but does not argue that negligible speedups today imply a longer wait for substantial acceleration.
